triage.name: Urinary Tract Infections
triage.reason: Very common infection with classic dysuria/frequency presentation, straightforward diagnosis by history, exam and urinalysis; important to distinguish cystitis from pyelonephritis.

age.peak: sexually active women 18–40; older adults with catheters or urologic disease

demographics: About four times as many women as men are affected
Very common in sexually active young women
Common in older adults, especially those in long-term care or with catheters
In men, often associated with instrumentation, obstruction or prostate disease

risk_factors.text: Female anatomy (short urethra, urethra near vagina and anus)
Sexual activity, especially with a new partner
Indwelling urinary catheter or recent instrumentation
Urinary obstruction or incomplete bladder emptying (BPH, stones, prolapse)
Spinal cord injury or neurogenic bladder
Family history of UTI in a first-degree relative

comorbidities: Neurogenic bladder or spinal cord injury
Dementia or functional impairment in older adults
family_history: UTIs in a mother or sister
social_history: Recent hospitalization or residence in a long-term care facility
Use of spermicides or a diaphragm

chief_complaints.text: I keep having to go to the bathroom
I feel like I have to pee all the time even right after I go
My urine smells bad and looks cloudy
I have pressure in my lower belly

hpi.onset: Usually abrupt over hours to a day or two
hpi.duration: Typically 1–3 days at presentation; symptoms often worsen without treatment
hpi.progression: Dysuria and urinary frequency come on quickly and persist; if the infection ascends to the kidney, fever, chills and flank pain develop
hpi.location: Burning along the urethra; suprapubic pressure or discomfort; flank or back pain if the upper tract is involved
hpi.radiation: Flank pain from pyelonephritis can radiate to the back or groin; bladder symptoms do not radiate
hpi.quality: Burning or stinging with urination; dull suprapubic pressure; constant, aching flank pain if upper tract
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for cystitis; moderate to severe with fever and flank pain in pyelonephritis
hpi.timing: Symptoms with every urination; frequency and urgency persist between voids
relieving: Nothing reliably; some relief after voiding
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen may take the edge off

associated_symptoms.text: Going to the bathroom much more often than usual
Blood in the urine (pink, red or tea-colored)
Flank or back pain below the ribs

pertinent_negatives: New or multiple sexual partners with discharge
Missed period or positive pregnancy test
Diarrhea or vomiting before urinary symptoms
Known kidney stones with colicky pain radiating to the groin

negatives: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to urinary symptoms
Difficulty starting the stream or dribbling
argues_against: Urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, weakness or decreased appetite rather than dysuria; fever may be absent.
Infants and young children may have only fever, irritability, poor feeding or vomiting; older children may have abdominal pain or new daytime wetting.
May be asymptomatic bacteriuria or present with mild symptoms; untreated infection carries risk of preterm labor and pyelonephritis.
Symptoms may be blunted and fever may be the only sign; risk of rapid progression to sepsis is higher.
More likely to have asymptomatic bacteriuria and complicated upper tract infection; symptoms may be milder than expected.
May have fewer urinary symptoms and more systemic signs; antibiotic dosing and follow-up need adjustment.

general.mild: Comfortable, non-toxic, no distress; may shift in the chair with bladder fullness
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, frequent trips to the bathroom, mild distress
general.severe: Ill-appearing, flushed, diaphoretic, lying still to avoid flank pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, mottled, lethargic or confused, signs of sepsis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the suprapubic region with a single hand
Percuss each costovertebral angle with the ulnar side of the fist
findings.finding: Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the flank below the ribs
Palpate all four quadrants and check for rebound or guarding
findings.finding: No rebound tenderness, guarding or rigidity

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam when vaginitis or pelvic inflammatory disease is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness, adnexal mass or abnormal discharge
No abnormal vaginal discharge, ulcers or vesicles

findings.maneuver: Inspect the urethral meatus and milk the urethra if discharge is suspected
Perform a digital rectal exam in men when prostatitis or obstruction is suspected
findings.finding: Prostate not exquisitely tender or boggy

findings.maneuver: Check neck stiffness and mental status when fever is present
findings.finding: No neck stiffness, normal mental status

labs.caveat: Leukocyte esterase reflects pyuria; it can be positive without infection and negative early in the course.
Specific for Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli; negative with gram-positive organisms, Pseudomonas or frequent voiding.
Pyuria supports UTI but is not specific; it also occurs with sterile inflammation and contamination.
Bacteria on urinalysis can reflect contamination; correlate with symptoms and culture.
Hematuria is common in UTI but also occurs with stones, tumors and glomerular disease.
Mild proteinuria is nonspecific; heavy or persistent proteinuria suggests glomerular disease rather than UTI.
Leukocytosis is more typical of pyelonephritis; a normal white count does not exclude infection.
A left shift suggests a more invasive infection such as pyelonephritis or early sepsis.
A rise in creatinine suggests dehydration, obstruction or kidney involvement; it also guides antibiotic dosing.
Elevated from dehydration or poor intake; a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 supports prerenal azotemia.
Elevation suggests sepsis from pyelonephritis and warrants urgent evaluation and fluids.
Supports upper tract involvement but is not needed for routine cystitis.
May help distinguish bacterial pyelonephritis from other causes of systemic illness; not routine.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or antibiotics that are unsafe in pregnancy.

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Complicated pyelonephritis, suspected obstruction, stone or abscess, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics

findings.text: Unilateral enlarged, edematous kidney with decreased enhancement
Wedge-shaped areas of reduced enhancement (focal pyelonephritis)
Renal or ureteral stone causing obstruction
Gas within the renal parenchyma (emphysematous pyelonephritis)

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy, children, renal impairment, or when obstruction is suspected and CT is not ideal

findings.text: Normal-appearing kidneys and bladder (does not exclude pyelonephritis)
Postvoid residual urine suggesting incomplete emptying

imaging.study: CT urogram or magnetic resonance urogram
imaging.preferred_when: Recurrent infection, suspected anatomic abnormality, or when a stone or tumor is being evaluated

findings.text: Bladder diverticulum or other anatomic abnormality
Usually nonspecific; may show a radio-opaque urinary stone

initial.why: First-line test; leukocyte esterase, nitrite, pyuria and bacteriuria support UTI
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or antibiotic selection
Leukocytosis and left shift suggest pyelonephritis or systemic infection
initial.only_if: fever, flank pain or systemic symptoms suggest upper tract infection

initial.why: Assesses hydration, kidney function and electrolytes; guides antibiotic dosing
initial.only_if: vomiting, dehydration, older adult or suspected kidney involvement

initial.why: Looks for obstruction, stone or abscess
initial.only_if: suspected obstruction, renal impairment, pregnancy, or failure to improve

confirmatory.why: Confirms the organism and guides therapy; essential in pyelonephritis, pregnancy, men, recurrent or complicated UTI, and when resistance is a concern

supporting.why: Screens for sepsis in ill-appearing patients with suspected pyelonephritis
supporting.only_if: hypotension, tachycardia, confusion or other signs of sepsis

supporting.why: Supports upper tract involvement when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: fever or flank pain without clear localizing signs

supporting.why: May help distinguish bacterial pyelonephritis from other systemic illness
supporting.only_if: diagnosis is unclear or sepsis is being considered

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Defines complications such as abscess, obstruction or emphysematous pyelonephritis
supporting.only_if: severe pyelonephritis, suspected abscess or stone, or no improvement after 48–72 hours of antibiotics

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated cystitis; exposes the patient to radiation and contrast
No role in the diagnosis of urinary tract infection
Not routine for cystitis or mild pyelonephritis; reserve for sepsis or critically ill patients
not_indicated.only_if: sepsis, hemodynamic instability or suspected bacteremia

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or antibiotic selection in anyone who could be pregnant
Distinguish cystitis from pyelonephritis by fever, chills and costovertebral angle tenderness; pyelonephritis needs a longer course and often culture
Urine culture before antibiotics in pyelonephritis, pregnancy, men, recurrent or complicated UTI
Image when there is suspected obstruction, abscess, stone, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
Consider sepsis and start fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics when hypotension, tachycardia, confusion or elevated lactate are present

differential.name: Urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection
differential.why_considered: Dysuria and urinary frequency in a sexually active young adult, especially with a new partner
differential.trigger: Urethral discharge, a new or multiple sexual partners, or dysuria without frequency or urgency

history: Symptoms begin gradually days to weeks after exposure
Dysuria without urinary frequency or urgency
exam: Urethral discharge on inspection or after milking the urethra
No suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness
labs: Urinalysis with pyuria but no nitrite and a negative urine culture
Positive nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia or gonorrhea

differential.name: Vaginitis
differential.why_considered: Burning with urination and vulvar discomfort in women

history: External burning rather than internal urethral burning
labs: Wet mount or vaginal pH showing yeast, clue cells or trichomonads

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain with urinary symptoms and fever in a sexually active woman
differential.trigger: Lower abdominal pain with fever, abnormal discharge, or cervical motion tenderness

exam: Lower abdominal tenderness without suprapubic localization
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia or gonorrhea
Elevated white blood cell count and inflammatory markers
Urinalysis may show pyuria but urine culture is negative
imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound showing thickened fallopian tubes, fluid-filled tube or tubo-ovarian complex

differential.name: Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)
differential.why_considered: Chronic urinary frequency, urgency and bladder pain that mimics recurrent UTI

imaging: Normal bladder and upper tracts on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Nephrolithiasis
differential.why_considered: Flank pain with nausea and blood in the urine

history: Sudden, severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Patient writhes and cannot get comfortable
No fever or dysuria at onset
exam: Costovertebral angle tenderness may be present
labs: Hematuria on urinalysis without pyuria or nitrite
imaging: Radio-opaque stone and hydronephrosis on noncontrast CT

differential.name: Acute bacterial prostatitis
differential.why_considered: Dysuria, frequency and pelvic pain in a man

exam: Exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on digital rectal exam

differential.name: Asymptomatic bacteriuria
differential.why_considered: Bacteria and pyuria on urinalysis in a patient without urinary symptoms

history: No dysuria, frequency, urgency or suprapubic pain
exam: No suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness

severity.mild: Uncomplicated cystitis: dysuria, frequency and urgency with low-grade or no fever, suprapubic tenderness only, and normal vital signs
severity.moderate: Cystitis with more marked symptoms or early pyelonephritis: fever, chills, flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness, with mild leukocytosis
severity.severe: Pyelonephritis with systemic illness: high fever, rigors, vomiting, tachycardia, dehydration and acute kidney injury
severity.critical: Urosepsis with hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, respiratory distress or organ dysfunction

red_flags.finding: High fever with rigors and flank pain
red_flags.meaning: Upper tract infection (pyelonephritis); needs longer treatment and urine culture
Sepsis from urosepsis; needs urgent fluids, cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Vomiting and inability to keep fluids or oral antibiotics down
red_flags.meaning: Dehydration and failure of oral therapy; consider admission and IV antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Rising creatinine or decreased urine output
red_flags.meaning: Kidney involvement or obstruction; image the urinary tract

red_flags.finding: Symptoms persisting or worsening after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Resistant organism, obstruction, abscess or an alternative diagnosis; image and reculture

red_flags.finding: Pregnancy with urinary symptoms or positive urine culture
red_flags.meaning: Risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labor; treat and follow up closely
Complicated infection; evaluate for obstruction or prostatic involvement

complications.name: Renal or perinephric abscess
clues: Persistent fever after 48–72 hours of antibiotics
Flank mass or severe localized pain

complications.name: Emphysematous pyelonephritis
clues: Gas within the renal parenchyma on CT

complications.name: Recurrent UTI
clues: Two or more infections in six months or three or more in a year

complications.name: Preterm labor and low birth weight
clues: Pregnancy with untreated bacteriuria or pyelonephritis

special_populations.differences: Infants and young children may present only with fever, irritability, poor feeding or vomiting; obtain a urine culture before antibiotics and consider ultrasound after a first febrile UTI.
Fever without a source is the usual presentation; bagged urine specimens are unreliable and catheterization or suprapubic aspiration is preferred for culture.
May present with confusion, falls, weakness or decreased appetite rather than dysuria; fever may be absent, and asymptomatic bacteriuria is common so symptoms must be confirmed before treating.
Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines; untreated infection risks pyelonephritis, preterm labor and low birth weight.
Symptoms may be blunted and fever may be the only sign; higher risk of rapid progression to sepsis and unusual organisms.
More likely to have asymptomatic bacteriuria and complicated upper tract infection, including emphysematous pyelonephritis; symptoms may be milder than expected.
May have fewer urinary symptoms and more systemic signs; adjust antibiotic doses and follow kidney function closely.

key_questions.question: What urinary symptoms are you having — burning, going more often, or a sudden urge to go?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria, frequency and urgency — the core symptoms of lower urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: When did these symptoms start, and are they getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset over hours to a day or two, worsening without treatment

key_questions.question: Do you have any fever, chills or shaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and rigors suggest upper tract infection (pyelonephritis) rather than simple cystitis

key_questions.question: Do you have pain in your back or side below the ribs?
key_questions.looking_for: Flank pain suggests pyelonephritis; its absence supports cystitis

key_questions.question: Have you felt nauseated or vomited?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting suggest systemic illness or upper tract involvement

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine, or that it looks cloudy or smells bad?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematuria, cloudy or malodorous urine support UTI but are nonspecific

key_questions.question: Have you had a urinary tract infection before, and how was it treated?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior UTIs, recent antibiotics and any resistant organisms

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, kidney stones, a spinal cord injury, or any trouble emptying your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that make the infection complicated or predispose to recurrence

key_questions.question: Do you have a urinary catheter or have you had any recent urinary procedures?
key_questions.looking_for: Catheter-associated or instrumented infection, which is often complicated

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active, and do you use spermicides or a diaphragm?
key_questions.looking_for: Sexual activity and spermicide use are strong risk factors; also raises the question of urethritis or vaginitis

key_questions.question: Have you had any vaginal discharge, itching or sores?
key_questions.looking_for: Present suggests vaginitis or a sexually transmitted infection rather than UTI

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes treatment and follow-up; also excludes ectopic pregnancy in a woman with pelvic pain

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications, especially SGLT2 inhibitors, steroids or immunosuppressants?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that increase UTI risk or affect antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Do you have any allergies to antibiotics, especially penicillins or sulfa drugs?
Have you been confused, very weak, or had any falls recently?
key_questions.looking_for: In older adults, confusion or falls may be the presenting sign of UTI or sepsis

reasoning_points: Dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency with suprapubic discomfort point to a lower urinary tract infection
Fever, chills, flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness indicate upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis)
Urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrite, pyuria and bacteriuria supports the diagnosis
Urine culture confirms the organism and guides therapy, especially in complicated, recurrent or upper tract infection
Pregnancy must be excluded before imaging or choosing antibiotics
Look-alikes such as urethritis, vaginitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, nephrolithiasis and interstitial cystitis are considered and excluded by history, exam and urinalysis
Red flags such as hypotension, confusion, vomiting or rising creatinine suggest sepsis or a complicated infection requiring urgent care

easy: Sexually active young woman with classic dysuria, frequency and urgency
No fever or flank pain, suprapubic tenderness only
Urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase, nitrite and pyuria
Clear response to a short course of antibiotics
medium: Older adult with confusion or falls but no dysuria
Man with dysuria and frequency suggesting prostatitis or obstruction
Pregnant patient with asymptomatic bacteriuria or mild symptoms
Patient with diabetes and a more complicated or upper tract infection
Symptoms overlap with vaginitis or a sexually transmitted infection
hard: Afebrile older adult with nonspecific weakness and a normal white count
Recurrent UTI with a resistant organism or anatomic abnormality
Pyelonephritis with obstruction, abscess or failure to improve after 48–72 hours
Urosepsis with hypotension, tachycardia and elevated lactate
Catheterized or spinal cord injury patient with blunted symptoms
